config.title: @supports

intro.title: @supports
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple webpage that uses the @supports rule to apply different styles based on browser support for specific CSS features. You will learn how to use @supports to check if a browser supports a CSS property or value, and then conditionally apply styles accordingly. The main technology involved is the CSS @supports at-rule, which allows you to write feature queries. This is a beginner-friendly introduction to creating more robust and forward-compatible CSS by gracefully handling browser differences.
intro.usecase: The @supports rule is essential for creating progressive enhancement strategies in modern web applications. Developers use it to conditionally apply CSS features like CSS Grid or Flexbox layouts in dashboards and data tables, ensuring they work across different browser versions. For example, a responsive admin panel might use @supports to implement advanced grid layouts in modern browsers while falling back to simpler float-based layouts in older ones. This pattern is also valuable for implementing cutting-edge UI features like CSS custom properties in design systems or backdrop-filter effects in modal dialogs, providing graceful degradation without breaking the user experience.

objectives: Apply @supports to test for CSS property support in a stylesheet
Construct conditional CSS rules that only execute when specific features are supported
Configure fallback styles using @supports to maintain compatibility across browsers
Implement @supports with logical operators (and, or, not) to test multiple features
Manipulate layout behavior by applying @supports to control advanced CSS features
Integrate @supports with modern CSS properties to progressively enhance designs
Update existing CSS code to include @supports for better cross-browser support

steps.title: Introduce the @supports rule
steps.instruction: Write a CSS comment explaining what the @supports rule is used for.
steps.hint: Start with /* and end with */ to create a comment. Mention that @supports tests browser support for CSS features.
steps.analogousExample: /* This is a CSS comment explaining a concept */
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS comment that describes the purpose of @supports.
successCriteria: The comment explains that @supports is a CSS at-rule used to test browser support for specific CSS features before applying styles.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've written a comment, but it doesn't fully explain what @supports does. Make sure to mention it's a CSS at-rule that tests browser support for CSS features.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look like a CSS comment explaining @supports. Remember to use /* and */ to create a comment that describes what @supports is used for.

steps.instruction: Write the basic @supports rule syntax: @supports (property: value) { /* styles */ }
steps.hint: Start with @supports followed by parentheses containing a CSS property and value test, then curly braces for the conditional styles.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have written the basic syntax structure for an @supports rule.
successCriteria: The code contains a valid @supports rule with the correct syntax: @supports (property: value) { /* styles */ }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have @supports followed by parentheses with a property: value test, then curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The syntax isn't quite right. Remember: @supports (property: value) { /* styles */ }

steps.expectedOutcome: The @supports rule now specifically tests for CSS Grid support.

steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the condition inside @supports specifically tests 'display: grid'.

steps.title: Add fallback styles outside @supports
steps.instruction: Add a fallback style for browsers that don't support CSS Grid by writing a CSS rule for .container with display: block before the @supports rule.
steps.hint: Place the fallback rule above the @supports rule. The fallback will apply first, then be overridden by the @supports block if the browser supports Grid.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS now has a fallback display: block rule for .container, placed before the @supports rule.
successCriteria: A .container rule with display: block exists above the @supports rule.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you added display: block for .container and placed it before the @supports rule.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fallback style is missing or incorrectly placed. Add .container { display: block; } above the @supports rule.

steps.title: Use @supports not to exclude browsers
steps.instruction: Add an @supports rule with the not operator to test for browsers that do NOT support display: grid. Place it after your existing @supports rule.
steps.hint: The syntax is @supports not (property: value). Use the same property-value pair you tested earlier (display: grid).
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have two @supports rules: one for browsers that support display: grid, and another for browsers that do NOT support it.
successCriteria: An @supports rule with the not operator is added, testing for not (display: grid).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you use the exact syntax @supports not (display: grid).
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires adding an @supports rule with the not operator. Check the syntax and try again.

steps.title: Combine conditions with and operator
steps.instruction: Write an @supports rule that tests for both 'display: grid' and 'grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr)' using the 'and' operator.
steps.hint: Use the syntax @supports (property1: value1) and (property2: value2) to combine multiple feature tests.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll create an @supports rule that checks for two CSS features simultaneously using the logical 'and' operator.
successCriteria: The code includes a valid @supports rule with the syntax @supports (display: grid) and (grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr)).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your @supports rule uses the exact syntax with parentheses around each condition and the 'and' keyword between them.
steps.feedbackWrong: The @supports rule with 'and' operator wasn't implemented correctly. Review the syntax: @supports (condition1) and (condition2).

steps.title: Combine conditions with or operator
steps.instruction: Write an @supports rule using the 'or' operator to test for alternative feature support. Add it after your existing CSS rules.
steps.hint: Use the syntax @supports (property1: value1) or (property2: value2) { /* styles */ } to apply styles if either condition is true.
steps.expectedOutcome: An @supports rule using the 'or' operator is added to test for alternative CSS feature support.
successCriteria: The code includes an @supports rule with the 'or' operator syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the correct 'or' operator syntax: @supports (property: value) or (property: value).
steps.feedbackWrong: The 'or' operator wasn't used correctly. Review the syntax: @supports (property: value) or (property: value) { /* styles */ }.
